decision.quote: To replicate the original thermal tolerance experiments conducted in 1970 ( Coles, Jokiel & Lewis, 1976 ; Jokiel & Coles, 1977 ; Coles & Jokiel, 1978 ), three species of corals, Montipora capitata (previously M. verrucosa ), Pocillopora damicornis, and Lobactis scutaria (previously Fungia scutaria ) , ( Gittenberger, Reijnen & Hoeksema, 2011 ) were collected from the Moku o Lo‘e reef in Kāne‘ohe Bay, O‘ahu, near the original 1970 experiment collection site (21.4°N, 157.8°W).
decision.reason: Addressing the prior scope objection: inspecting all citations and results shows that Coles, Jokiel & Lewis (1976, 'Thermal tolerance in tropical versus subtropical pacific reef corals') is cited in Introduction and Methodology only within grouped references to the 1970s research series and for observer SLC's visual assessment experience, and is never cited in Results. Its specific finding is identified in Discussion as 'a shift upward of ~2.0 °C in thermal tolerances of Enewetak compared to Hawaiian corals that is related to the long-term temperature environments of the two regions ( Coles, Jokiel & Lewis, 1976 )', which is used as a regional analogy rather than empirically re-tested here (only Hawaiian corals from Kāne‘ohe Bay were tested in 2017). All 1970-versus-2017 empirical comparisons in Results (30-day calcification, survivorship, and bleaching onset across L. scutaria, M. capitata, and P. damicornis, n = 20 in 1970) refer in the singular to 'the Jokiel and Coles 1970 experiment' already represented by Jokiel & Coles (1977) in shipped row 729.

decision.quote: Irradiance has been documented to have a significant influence on coral growth, bleaching, and mortality ( Jokiel & Coles, 1977 ; Coles & Jokiel, 1978 ; Hoegh-Guldberg & Smith, 1989 ; Goenaga & Canals, 1990 ; Fitt & Warner, 1995 ; Brown et al., 1999 ; Jokiel, 2004 ). Our investigation of response across irradiance levels determined that irradiance plays a key role in the recovery of corals. Corals exposed to identical temperatures with a 50% reduction in irradiance had a 17% lower mortality rate than those at full light exposure. However, calcification rates did not differ across irradiance levels during either the stress or recovery periods.
decision.reason: Addressing the prior scope objection regarding irradiance: Coles & Jokiel (1978, 'Synergistic effects of temperature, salinity and light on the hermatypic coral Montipora verrucosa') studied temperature, salinity, and light interactions in M. verrucosa alone, whereas the 2017 study did not manipulate salinity and did not compare its 50% shading manipulation against any 1970/1978 irradiance data. In the 2017 experiment, irradiance had no effect on calcification during the stress or recovery period (p = 0.442) and affected partial mortality only during the 28-day recovery period (p = 0.016), for which the authors note 'no recovery measurements were reported from 1970'. All 1970-versus-2017 empirical comparisons in Results (Figs. 4-6, Table 3) are restricted to ambient/full-sun irradiance across all three species from the 30-day experiment represented by Jokiel & Coles (1977) in shipped row 729, while Coles & Jokiel (1978) is cited in Results solely for historical tank temperature standard deviations (0.9-1.2 °C) and in Discussion as part of a seven-paper background list on irradiance.

decision.quote: Additionally, whole-colony mortality was observed sooner, just after 3 days of exposure to 31 °C, in 1970 (i.e., P. damicornis, n = 15; M. capitata, n = 8; and L. scutaria, n = 3) ( Jokiel et al., 1975 ) (Wilcoxon rank-sum test: L. scutaria p <0.0001; M. capitata p < 0.0001; P. damicornis p < 0.0001). Corals were able to withstand elevated temperatures (31.4 °C) for a longer period of time in the current 2017 experiment.
decision.reason: Addressing the prior scope objection: Jokiel et al. (1975, 'Effects of thermal loading on Hawaiian reef corals', EPA Ecological Research Series technical report, 285 pp.) is not an independent original study but the comprehensive EPA technical report for the same 1970 Hawaiian coral thermal-loading experiment whose mortality and growth results were published in the peer-reviewed journal article Jokiel & Coles (1977) (shipped row 729). In Results, both the 30-day survivorship and ambient control data cited to Jokiel & Coles (1977) and the day-3 whole-colony mortality counts at 31 °C (n = 15, n = 8, n = 3 out of n = 20 per species) cited to Jokiel et al. (1975) describe and are plotted on the same 1970 survivorship curves in Figure 5 ('comparison of the Jokiel and Coles 1970 experiment with the current experiment'). Under the codebook and review instructions, a technical report version of the same original work already captured by its published journal article in shipped row 729 is represented.

decision.quote: Existing research finds that weapons that eliminate the possibility of military casualties, such as drones, increase popular support for engaging in conflict. We argue that this effect may be overstated because the choice of weapons technology is endogenous to conflict. Leaders may select to use drones in conflicts where the risk of harm to ground forces is especially high. To address this, we replicate and extend the research design of Walsh and Schulzke across three survey experiments.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The blind target ('Walsh and Schulzke', with empty year, title, and DOI because the available source text consists solely of the article header and abstract without a reference list) refers to the exact original study already represented in shipped row 538: Walsh and Schulzke (2018), 'Drones and Support for the Use of Force' (DOI: 10.3998/mpub.9946611). The abstract explicitly states the original finding ('weapons that eliminate the possibility of military casualties, such as drones, increase popular support for engaging in conflict'), states that the authors 'replicate and extend the research design of Walsh and Schulzke across three survey experiments', and reports that support does not differ between drone strikes and ground troops. Because this original study is already present in shipped row 538 and went unmatched only due to missing bibliographic fields in the abstract-only source text, no target is missing.

corrected_value.title: Continuous hand movement induces a far-hand bias in attentional priority.

decision.quote: Based on the MVP hypothesis, we predicted improving temporal gap discrimination and impaired spatial gap detection as the hand approached the probe as compared to when the hand moves away from the probe. Furthermore, on the basis of the direction effect of Festman et al. (2013a , b ), we predicted better discrimination when moving toward the probe in both tasks.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The paper empirically re-tests the movement direction effect (superior visual discrimination when the hand moves toward versus away from a visual probe during continuous hand movement below the display) originally reported by Festman et al. (2013a, Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics 75:644-649, DOI: 10.3758/s13414-013-0430-4). The authors explicitly predict this direction effect in both temporal (Experiment 1) and spatial (Experiment 2) gap discrimination tasks, test Direction (toward vs. away) in their repeated-measures ANOVAs, and conclude in Results and Discussion that Experiment 2 reproduced and provided 'a replication of the previously established directionality effects in spatial tasks ( Festman et al., 2013a , b )' while Experiment 1 showed no modulation by movement direction. Shipped row 2153 (Gozli, West & Pratt, 2012, DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2012.04.008) is a different study testing static hand proximity (near vs. far) under the modulated visual pathways hypothesis, and sibling target_index 2 (Festman et al., 2013b, DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00657) is a separate subsequent empirical article examining the interplay of a stationary left hand and moving right hand.
